newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's tough guy minister faces biggest fight.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's tough guy minister faces biggest fight.

text.p: Sergio Motta, the Brazilian minister at the center of a cash-for-votes scandal, has long relished his role as the government's tough guy, but now he is fighting for his political life, observers said on Thursday.

In a series of reports this week, Folha de Sao Paulo daily published telephone conversations between two lawmakers and an unnamed "Mr X" which suggested Communications Minister Motta gave lawmakers cash and a television concession for their votes.

The minister, an old friend of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso and the most influential member of his cabinet, has denied he was involved in an irregularities in mustering support for the bill that would allow Cardoso to stand for re-election.

"The transcript of the conversation does not contain a single real fact or a concrete accusation," Motta said in a statement on Thursday, after the latest Folha report. "The facts mentioned are absurd, untruthful and I would say, surreal."

Motta is seldom out of the headlines, thanks to his outspoken views which have recently offended bishops, key allies in Congress and even the president's wife. He said she indulged in "sociological masturbation" as the head of a government social program.

Time and again, Cardoso has forgiven his former campaign manager, once dubbing him "a force of nature" which could not be controlled. "Motta is the dark shadow behind the president," said political consultant Ricardo Pedreira. "While Cardoso seeks the consensus, he is the one who plays hard."

Their friendship goes back to the late 1960's when Motta, then a successful businessman noted for his active opposition to the military dictatorship, gave financial support to a free-thinking research institute set up by Cardoso.

Congress-watchers say Motta's response to the Folha reports has been uncharacteristically low key, perhaps to avoid further aggravation of an already tense situation. But should new allegations surface, not even his special relationship with the president might be enough to save his job.
"Most people in Congress think he will survive but things will get very tricky if there are any more nasty reports," said Tereza Cruvinel, a political columnist with daily O Globo.

Newspapers despatched scores of reporters to the remote Amazonian state of Acre to investigate five lawmakers who were reported to have taken the bribes. The governors of Acre and neighboring Amazonas state were also mentioned in the report.
Financial markets in Sao Paulo, which fell earlier this week on Folha's stories, were awash with rumors of new allegations late on Thursday, traders said.

Motta, who is in charge of the upcoming $35 billion privatization of Brazil's telecommunications industry, is one of the darlings of local and foreign investors who like his enthusiasm for pro-market policies.
Even left-wing politicians demanding his head have respect for the man known as The Tractor.

"Personally, I think Sergio Motta is the government's clearest political thinker but he seems to have gone over the top this time to get the re-election bill approved," said Workers Party deputy Milton Temer.
